result.text:
I didn't add an ETA cache, and I didn't change the endpoint code. The list handler turned out not to be slow, so there was nothing to speed up. All 95 tests pass: the 94 from before plus one new one.

**Why no cache:** QA already found a cached ETA going stale after a new event, and the ledger records that as a dead end. A cache would also save very little. I measured 5,000 shipments locally:

| Step | Time |
|---|---|
| `listShipments({limit: 50})` (copy and sort of all 5k) | about 0.2 ms |
| 50-item list with ETAs | about 0.5 ms |
| 500-item list with ETAs | about 2.4 ms |

The sort over all 5k shipments and the ETA calculation together cost less than 3 ms, even at `limit=500`. The slowness on staging comes from somewhere else. The 12 November log showed 166–348 ms for `GET /shipments?limit=50` with only about 30 shipments and no ETA in the response, which also points away from the ETA.

**What I added:** one test in `test/shipments-list-eta.test.ts`. It creates a shipment and reads its list ETA. It then posts an `exception` event and checks that the list ETA moved and matches `GET /shipments/:id`. Any future speedup has to keep passing it. I didn't add a timing test, because those fail intermittently.

**What I'd do next:**
1. Add timing to the request log. It already records `duration_ms`. Per-phase timing in the list handler (store, ETA, serialization) would show where the 166–348 ms goes on staging.
2. Look at the staging environment itself. The data file is on a bind mount, and I haven't ruled out disk I/O or logging there.
3. Build pagination as planned. A cursor on `created_at` would also stop the full copy and sort of all 5k on each request.

I haven't updated the ledger with this measurement yet, since you didn't ask for it.
